clue.text: Shakespearian footballer ?

definitions.meaning: Harry Percy, nicknamed for his fiery temper, is a character in Henry IV Part 1
a player for the Tottenham club of north London, whose full name carries this word

explanation.surface: A footballer who might have stepped out of a Shakespeare play.
explanation.walkthrough: Tottenham Hotspur is a London football club, so any of its players can be called by its name.
explanation.definitionFit: One sense is the hot-tempered rebel Harry Percy in Shakespeare; the other is a player for the Spurs football club.

clue.text: Hophead has his first

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

indicators.note: the first letter of the word Hophead is taken

explanation.surface: A drug user gets his first fix.
explanation.walkthrough: 'first' takes only the opening letter of 'Hophead', which goes at the end after HAS and HIS. The whole clue also describes an addict's first drug.
explanation.definitionFit: A hophead is slang for a drug addict, and cannabis resin is the drug such a person takes first.

clue.text: A bite of this, and you'll want to dance

definitions.text: A bite of this, and you'll want to dance

parts.words: A bite of this, and you'll want to dance
parts.note: folklore said the bite of a certain spider caused a dancing mania, from which the tarantella dance got its name

explanation.surface: Something whose bite sets you dancing.
explanation.walkthrough: In southern Italian folklore the bite of this spider caused tarantism, a frenzy cured by dancing the tarantella.
explanation.definitionFit: Legend links this big hairy spider's bite with the frantic dance named after the town of Taranto.

clue.text: Does he keep quiet when debagged ?

definitions.text: Does he keep quiet when debagged ?

parts.words: Does he keep quiet when debagged ?
parts.note: debagged usually means having one's trousers pulled off, but here it means losing the bag of a set of bagpipes, which then cannot sound

explanation.walkthrough: 'Debagged' is British slang for having one's trousers removed as a prank; here a bagpipe player loses the bag of the instrument, so he can make no noise.
explanation.definitionFit: A bagpipe player cannot sound a note without the instrument's bag.

clue.text: Characteristic of an all-rounder?

parts.note: an all-rounder in cricket can bat and bowl, but here it is read as a person round all over, that is, plump

explanation.walkthrough: In cricket an all-rounder is a player good at both batting and bowling; the clue reads the word as someone round in every direction.
explanation.definitionFit: Roundness or plumpness is the quality of being round all over.

clue.text: Tie a dog, if unruly, in the garden

indicators.note: unruly means disorderly, so the letters of the words before are put out of order

explanation.surface: Someone tethers a misbehaving dog out in the garden.
explanation.walkthrough: 'if unruly' rearranges TIEADOG. The definition is loose: this is a flower found in the garden.
explanation.definitionFit: This annual with showy pink or mauve blooms is a common garden flower.

clue.text: Just the kid to shine

parts.note: kid here is the soft leather from a young goat, and this kind is finished with a glossy surface

explanation.walkthrough: 'Kid' looks like a child, but it is goatskin leather; glacé kid is the glossy, polished kind.
explanation.definitionFit: The French word for glazed or iced names the glossy finish given to kid leather.

clue.text: Waste it — you don't want it in the kitchen

definitions.text: Waste it — you don't want it in the kitchen

parts.words: Waste it — you don't want it in the kitchen
parts.note: the dirty water left after washing up is waste poured away from the sink

explanation.surface: Advice to throw something away because it has no place in the kitchen.
explanation.walkthrough: After washing up, the dirty water is poured away: nobody wants to keep it.
explanation.definitionFit: Water used for washing plates is waste that is tipped down the drain.

clue.text: Not what Jaques meant by the Seven Ages of Man

definitions.text: Not what Jaques meant by the Seven Ages of Man

parts.words: Not what Jaques meant by the Seven Ages of Man
parts.note: in As You Like It Jaques describes seven stages of life; the clue thinks instead of the seven years from thirteen to nineteen

explanation.surface: A remark about the famous speech on the stages of life in As You Like It.
explanation.walkthrough: Jaques's 'All the world's a stage' speech lists seven stages of life; the seven ages whose names end in -teen, thirteen to nineteen, are another set.
explanation.definitionFit: Adolescence covers the seven years whose names end in -teen.

clue.text: Goddess is not quite a beginner

indicators.note: not quite means falling a little short, so the last letter of the word is dropped

parts.note: a beginner is a starter, someone just starting out

explanation.surface: A goddess who is very nearly a novice.
explanation.walkthrough: The page prints 'a', which the OCR read as '8'. 'not quite' drops the last letter of STARTER, leaving STARTE after A.
explanation.definitionFit: The Phoenician goddess of fertility and love is a deity of the ancient Near East.

clue.text: A narrow piece for the landing

definitions.text: A narrow piece for the landing

parts.words: A narrow piece for the landing
parts.note: a long narrow stretch of ground where aircraft touch down, rather than the landing at the top of a staircase

explanation.surface: A narrow piece of carpet for the top of the stairs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Landing' suggests the top of a staircase; it is an aircraft landing.
explanation.definitionFit: An airstrip is a long narrow piece of ground for aircraft to touch down on.

clue.text: Shakespearian doll

parts.note: Doll is a woman's first name here, the tavern prostitute in Henry IV Part 2, not a toy

explanation.walkthrough: 'doll' looks like a toy, but it is the first name of the prostitute Doll in Henry IV Part 2; her surname is the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Doll Tearsheet is Falstaff's companion at the Boar's Head tavern in Shakespeare.

clue.text: There's no knowing where this might be displayed

definitions.text: There's no knowing where this might be displayed

parts.words: There's no knowing where this might be displayed
parts.note: the phrase 'no knowing' normally means one cannot tell, but here it literally describes a lack of knowledge

explanation.surface: Nobody can say where the item will turn up on show.
explanation.walkthrough: 'There's no knowing' reads as 'one cannot tell'; taken literally, a state of no knowledge is what gets displayed.
explanation.definitionFit: Lack of knowledge, displayed wherever someone shows they do not know, is the sense.

clue.text: One up on the Magi ?

parts.note: the Magi are the Three Wise Men, so anyone better than them would be more wise

explanation.walkthrough: The Magi are traditionally called the Wise Men, so someone one up on them is more wise.
explanation.definitionFit: The comparative of the Magi's epithet describes someone with more good sense.

clue.text: "I walk my beat before London Town, Five — up and seven down." (Kipling)

definitions.text: "I walk my beat before London Town, Five — up and seven down." (Kipling)

parts.words: "I walk my beat before London Town, Five — up and seven down." (Kipling)
parts.note: Kipling's riddle-verse describes something like a watchman, but the beat is the swing of a clock's hand moving round

explanation.surface: A Kipling verse spoken by something that patrols its beat in front of London.
explanation.walkthrough: The lines are from Kipling's riddle 'The Hour' style verse: the clock face shows five of these on the way up and seven on the way down, twelve in all.
explanation.definitionFit: A clock face counts these twelve divisions, five rising on one side and seven falling on the other.

clue.text: Not possibly made of pig skin

definitions.text: Not possibly made of pig skin

parts.words: Not possibly made of pig skin
parts.note: this refers to the proverb that you cannot make a fine bag from a sow's ear

explanation.surface: Something that could never be fashioned from pigskin.
explanation.walkthrough: The proverb says you can't make a silk purse out of a sow's ear: nothing fine from poor material.
explanation.definitionFit: The proverb says this luxury item cannot be made from a sow's ear, so pig skin is no material for it.

clue.text: Evidently it isn't attention that upsets the soldier

definitions.text: Evidently it isn't attention that upsets the soldier

parts.words: Evidently it isn't attention that upsets the soldier
parts.note: a soldier's drill command opposite to standing at attention is the relaxed one; doing that badly is a state of discomfort

explanation.surface: A soldier is evidently unsettled by something other than standing to attention.
explanation.walkthrough: 'At ease' is the drill order opposite to 'attention', so a soldier upset by it is doing 'at ease' badly, feeling uncomfortable.
explanation.definitionFit: Uncomfortable or nervous is the sense, read as being poorly relaxed on the parade-ground command.

clue.text: Lord Ronald brought her a lily-white doe

definitions.text: Lord Ronald brought her a lily-white doe

parts.words: Lord Ronald brought her a lily-white doe
parts.note: the line quotes Tennyson's ballad in which Lord Ronald courts his cousin with this gift

explanation.surface: A nobleman presents a woman with a pure white deer.
explanation.walkthrough: The line is from Tennyson's ballad of that name, which opens with Lord Ronald bringing his cousin a white doe.
explanation.definitionFit: The heroine of Tennyson's ballad receives the lily-white doe from her lover Lord Ronald.

clue.text: Eric, about to depart after all, describes Pilgrim's Progress

indicators.note: after says the Eric piece comes behind the word all

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: about means going round, so the name Eric is placed around the word for departing

parts.note: taken as written
to depart is to go

explanation.surface: Someone called Eric, about to leave, gives an account of Bunyan's book.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' puts GO inside ERIC, making EGORIC, and 'after' sets that behind ALL.
explanation.definitionFit: Bunyan's Pilgrim's Progress is an extended symbolic tale, so a word for symbolic storytelling describes it.

clue.text: There's certainly no mix-up here

parts.note: mix-up suggests confusion, but it means mixing of metals, so a pure metal has none

explanation.surface: A reassurance that nothing has been confused.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mix-up' reads as confusion; it is mixing, as of metals in an alloy, so the answer is pure and unmixed.
explanation.definitionFit: Pure, unmixed metal has no alloy blended into it.

clue.text: Made run, perhaps lacking a weapon

indicators.note: perhaps means the letters might be arranged in some other way

explanation.surface: Someone was made to flee, maybe because he had no weapon.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' rearranges MADERUN.
explanation.definitionFit: Being without arms means having no weapon.

clue.text: Parts of the stage

parts.note: parts suggests physical sections of a stage, but here it is the characters actors play

explanation.walkthrough: 'Parts' looks like sections of the stage itself; it means the characters played on it.
explanation.definitionFit: Theatrical parts are the characters an actor takes on.

clue.text: But Hamlet's last word is meant to be heard

definitions.text: But Hamlet's last word is meant to be heard

parts.words: But Hamlet's last word is meant to be heard
parts.note: Hamlet dies saying 'The rest is' this word, which means the absence of sound, yet the actor speaks it for all to hear

explanation.surface: A theatrical point that the Prince's dying words must carry to the audience.
explanation.walkthrough: Hamlet's dying line is 'The rest is silence': its last word means no sound, but the actor must speak it audibly.
explanation.definitionFit: Absence of sound is what Hamlet's final word names, though the actor must voice it.

clue.text: This writer's output was fabulous

parts.note: fabulous normally means wonderful, but here it means consisting of fables

explanation.walkthrough: 'fabulous' looks like praise; it means made of fables, the Greek storyteller's whole output.
explanation.definitionFit: The ancient Greek storyteller is famous for his moral animal fables.

clue.text: Where the mails are sorted in India

definitions.text: Where the mails are sorted in India

indicators.note: sorted means put into a new order, so the letters of the word mails are rearranged

explanation.surface: A postal sorting office somewhere in India.
explanation.walkthrough: 'are sorted' rearranges MAILS; the whole clue also says where in India this happens.
explanation.definitionFit: The hill station, now spelt Shimla, was the summer capital of British India.

clue.text: Of a governor suggesting wickedness in high places ?

parts.note: vice is wickedness or immoral conduct
royal, as of those in the highest places, is regal

explanation.surface: Something about a governor that hints at corruption at the top.
explanation.walkthrough: VICE (wickedness) and REGAL (royal, the highest of places) join to give the adjective for a viceroy.
explanation.definitionFit: A viceroy governs a colony on behalf of the monarch, and this adjective describes such a governor.

clue.text: The only lady in solar orbit

definitions.text: The only lady in solar orbit

parts.words: The only lady in solar orbit
parts.note: of the planets circling the sun, just one is named after a female deity

explanation.surface: A woman who alone is travelling round the sun.
explanation.walkthrough: All the other planets are named after male gods; only one bears a goddess's name.
explanation.definitionFit: The second planet from the sun is the only one named after a goddess.

clue.text: This rent is payable more than once

definitions.text: This rent is payable more than once

parts.words: This rent is payable more than once
parts.note: rent suggests money for a home, but the clue means something that keeps falling due again

explanation.surface: A rent that has to be paid repeatedly.
explanation.walkthrough: Rent falls due again and again, which is what the answer means: to happen repeatedly.
explanation.definitionFit: To come round again and again is what a regular payment does.

clue.text: Don't forget those notes

parts.note: the Latin plural means things to be remembered, written notes kept as reminders

explanation.surface: A reminder to remember some notes.
explanation.walkthrough: The Latin word means 'things to be remembered', so the notes themselves say 'don't forget'.
explanation.definitionFit: These written reminders take their name from Latin for things that must be remembered.

clue.text: Shakespearian shepherd

parts.note: an old shepherd in the Forest of Arden in As You Like It

explanation.walkthrough: The old shepherd in As You Like It.
explanation.definitionFit: The aged shepherd of the Forest of Arden appears in As You Like It.

clue.text: Timber merchants, maybe ?

parts.note: deal is pine or fir wood, so those trading in it could be named after the wood, though the word usually means traders in general

explanation.walkthrough: Deal is a British word for softwood planks of pine or fir, so merchants selling it might be named after it.
explanation.definitionFit: Traders in general are named this, and in timber, deal is softwood.

clue.text: A race he made a hash of painfully

definitions.text: A race he made a hash of painfully

indicators.note: making a hash of something means muddling it, so the letters are jumbled

explanation.surface: A runner botched a race while in pain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'made a hash of' rearranges AACEHER; the whole clue also suggests a painful run.
explanation.definitionFit: A painful ache inside the head's hearing organ makes a hash of a race for anyone suffering it.
